title: The Con Artist Who Sold An Imaginary Country For Millions
sources: The Economist / David Sinclair 'The Land That Never Was' - In 1820, Scottish officer Gregor MacGregor claimed the title 'Cazique of Poyais' and invented a fictional Central American nation.
Bank of England Archives - MacGregor issued 200,000 pounds in Poyais government land certificates and loans in London, sending 250 British settlers to an unsettled wilderness in 1822.

lines.text: In eighteen twenty, a Scottish general made millions of dollars by selling an entire country -
lines.caps: In 1820, | a Scottish general | made millions | selling a country -

lines.text: that did not exist anywhere on Earth.
Gregor MacGregor claimed he was the official sovereign prince of Poyais,
a mythical paradise in Central America loaded with fertile gold mines and exotic timber.
He printed glossy guidebooks, opened a fake Poyais embassy in London, and invented his own national currency.
British investors scrambled to buy government bonds, handing MacGregor over two hundred thousand pounds.
Two hundred and fifty eager settlers sold everything they owned and boarded ships for their new tropical life.
When they landed, there were no cities, no farms, and no gold mines.
Just an untamed, malaria-infested swamp where dozens of settlers died before rescue ships arrived.
Back in Europe, MacGregor slipped across the border to France and immediately started selling Poyais bonds all over again!
One of the greatest real estate frauds in human history, built on pure imagination.
